replies:
Short answer: probably not yet. Quitting before you have another offer eliminates your leverage, creates income gaps that make job hunting harder, and removes legal or benefits protections (unemployment, COBRA, references). But there are valid exceptions. I’ll give the quick trade-offs, a practical checklist to protect you now, and one next step.
Trade-offs
- Staying (while you look): keeps pay/benefits, makes you look stable to employers, lets you search from a position of strength, and gives time to negotiate offers. Downside: ongoing stress, possible mental health harms, continued poor references if things escalate.
- Quitting now: removes daily stress immediately and may be necessary if the workplace is unsafe (harassment, threats, violence) or seriously harming your health. Downside: longer job search, lower immediate bargaining power, potential gaps on resume, loss of employer-sponsored benefits, and limited unemployment eligibility.
When quitting first makes sense (consider quitting now if any of these apply)
- You face physical danger, credible threats, or sustained harassment that HR won’t fix.
- A clinician (doctor/therapist) advises you to stop for mental/physical health reasons and documents it.
- You’ve saved 3–6 months of living expenses, have reliable contacts who can hire you quickly, or have an independent income source.
- Continuing would cause irreparable professional harm (forced to do illegal or fraudulent acts).
If none of those apply, do this instead (practical checklist)
1) Document incidents: dates, what was said/done, witnesses, and any written records (emails, messages). This helps HR, unemployment, or legal steps later.
2) Protect your finances: build a 1–3 month emergency buffer if possible; map monthly burn and benefits you’d lose.
3) Quiet job search: update resume, LinkedIn, and target 2–3 companies/roles; set alerts. I can search and queue applications when you say what role/location/seniority you want.
4) Use supports: talk with HR if you want (but be cautious if they’re aligned with your boss), or get confidential advice from an employment lawyer or union rep if applicable.
5) Prepare an exit strategy: ideal timeline, notice length, how to hand off work, who to notify for references.
6) Self-care plan: time off, therapy sessions, or a short leave if your doctor can support it.

If you want to act now, tell me the single most important piece of missing info and I’ll take the next step:
- Do you feel physically unsafe or are you being harassed/threatened? (Yes/No)
If yes, I’ll tell you how to document it and optional immediate protections. If no, I’ll help craft a quiet job search plan targeted to the role and location you want.
items.note: Meets requirements: directly addresses quitting before having another offer, lists practical trade-offs including runway/timeline and job-search-while-employed, and offers to help start a search with a clear next-step question.

Short answer: maybe — it depends on your role, career goal, industry and the jobs you want next.
Quick checklist to decide if PMP is worth it for you:
- Current role: Are you already managing projects or expected to in 1–2 years? PMP helps more if you lead cross-functional projects, budgets, vendors, timelines.
- Target roles: Do the job listings you want explicitly list “PMP” or “Project Management Professional” as required or preferred? If yes, it raises your chance. If they prefer Agile/Scrum only, consider CSM/PSM instead.
- Industry: Construction, defense, government, engineering, pharmaceuticals and large enterprises often value PMP. Startups and pure-software teams often value delivery experience and Agile certifications more.
- Experience eligibility: PMP requires 36 months (with bachelor’s) or 60 months (without) of leading projects plus 35 hours of PDUs / training. Do you already meet that? If not, the CAPM or agile cert might be more practical.
- Employer support: Will your employer pay or allow study time? Employer-backed PMPs are lower-cost and easier.
- ROI timeframe: Expect 3–5 years to recoup time/cost via higher pay or better roles. It’s stronger as a signal when combined with demonstrable project outcomes on your resume.
- Alternatives: For product/tech roles, consider Certified ScrumMaster, PMI-ACP, or demonstrating delivery via quantified project results. For entry-level PM paths, CAPM is cheaper.
Concrete next step I can do for you now:
- If you want, I’ll check current job postings you’d apply to and report how many list PMP as required/preferred. That will tell us whether it’s worth the investment for your market. Say the job title and location (or “remote”) you’re targeting. One question: which title and location should I check?

2) Immediate actions (next 30 days)
- Ask [your store leader title or name] for a short development chat. Say: “I want to grow into a Team Lead role — can you tell me the specific gaps you see and one thing I can do this week to show readiness?” Take notes, follow up on the exact items they give you.
- Volunteer for shift lead duties when a leader is short or ask to be a backup on a shift to run register teams, handle cash overviews, or lead huddles.
- Master daily operational tasks: pull lists, backroom flow, register audits, price changes, POD scanning — be the person who notices and fixes operational gaps.
- Improve measurable performance: hit or beat scan rate/units per hour targets relevant to your area, reduce errors, and maintain perfect attendance for scheduled shifts (or be proactive about coverage).

3) Skill & proof building (30–90 days)
- Run at least 5 shifts where you perform clear lead tasks (open/close, huddles, task delegation, incidents). Ask [a store leader] to observe one and give feedback.

- Request and complete any available Target leadership or role-specific training (Talents & Learning modules, RedCard, basic compliance modules). Note completions.
- Improve guest scores and peer feedback: politely ask a peer or leader for short written feedback after a shift you led (“Can you note 1 thing I did well and 1 thing I can improve?”). Keep three recent positive notes.

5) Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
- Pitfall: waiting passively. Fix: proactively seek tasks and feedback.
- Pitfall: poor attendance/availability. Fix: keep a clean attendance record and offer flexible coverage.
- Pitfall: weak relationships with peers. Fix: model respect, help teammates, communicate clearly when delegating.

- Pick one visible problem area (e.g., returns line, backstock accuracy) and own a clear, measurable fix over 2–4 weeks. Present results to [your store leader].
